question: Which prospects seem most likely to purchase, based on the conversations?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every buying signal and purchase-intent indicator in this call: expressed interest or enthusiasm, stated budget or budget approval, timeline or deadline for a decision, named decision makers and approval process, requests for proposal, pricing or contract discussion, pilot or trial requests, agreed next steps, and objections or blockers that could stop a purchase. Quote the relevant statements and note whether the prospect or OrbitFlow staff made them.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as calls of type Prospect (new business), excluding renewals, churned customers and cold calls.
Likelihood to purchase is a judgement across calls, so each call is read for underlying buying signals rather than a ranking.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows
findings.context: Customer expressed interest in testing the product: will supply three real workflows if given a sandbox. — Pilot request and buying signal from the prospect after the call; conditional on exception handling holding up.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: That's the intent. It'll slip. It always slips. But that's the plan.
findings.context: Customer stated a timeline: choose a vendor before end of July and first workflows live in September, but acknowledged it will slip. — Timeline and decision deadline; Maya's question framed the date, Rachel confirmed it as the intent.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected.
findings.context: Pricing was discussed: Growth tier starts at $1,800/month for up to thirty users on an annual agreement; Enterprise is custom. Customer said it was more than expected and benchmarked against Zapier. — Price objection/cost concern; customer says it may still be justifiable if it replaces manual work and some Gainsight spend.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story
findings.context: Customer said the price could still be justified only with a clearer ROI story, so cost is a blocker unless ROI is made concrete. — Objection tied to cost; customer also named potential offset from Gainsight spend.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
findings.context: Main commercial blocker: customer must win internally on expanding its existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Competing alternative and internal approval risk, raised as the real commercial question.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I own the project. IT security and the VP of Customer Success sign off. Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year
findings.context: Decision process: Rachel owns the project; IT security and the VP of Customer Success sign off; finance is involved above $25,000 a year. — Named decision makers and approval thresholds.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Customer set conditions for moving to a decision: a working representative workflow with real data, security gates understood, a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises, and an operating team that believes it can own it. — Explicit decision criteria and objections that could stop purchase.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Customer asked that per-seat licensing be explicit, worried that occasional approvers would need full seats. — Licence and per-seat pricing concern; OrbitFlow agreed to itemise builders and viewer/approver populations.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: a perfectly valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said pricing would be itemised and the exact seat number deliberately withheld until the user model is known; a 'don't buy' outcome was framed as valid. — Vendor position on pricing and purchase; vendor framed the pilot against status quo and Workato.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
findings.context: Next steps agreed: vendor sends security pack and architecture summary; customer sends representative workflow and sample data; jointly write three to five pilot success criteria before deciding on sandbox. — Agreed next steps toward a pilot.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
findings.context: Tom Alvarez wants the pilot to show reliability and ongoing maintainability before buying, and framed the honest comparison as Workato or improving the status quo. — Buying objection/criteria from a second decision-side stakeholder.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction.
findings.context: Customer said the ROI case cannot be framed as headcount reduction; the stronger case is consistency and speed. — ROI framing for internal approval.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
findings.context: Security review is not a blocker; the customer said the gating issue is not security, and Tom said AI concerns should not block the automation case. — Objection assessment; AI security review could be separated.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data. But I want to be explicit about something: a successful pilot would not automatically mean we can deploy broadly.
findings.context: BrightPath's sponsor would still consider a limited pilot, but a successful pilot does not automatically mean broad deployment; these are two decisions with different approvers. — Buying signal tempered by explicit separation of pilot vs. broad deployment decisions.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Prospect's stated decision gate: the BAA is a hard gate; without one, OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow that may involve PHI. — Primary blocker to any purchase; security/BAA must be answered before pricing matters.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
findings.context: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security confirms whether the BAA requirement can be met; price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Pricing/contract discussion deferred; objection to commercial discussion now.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Honestly? I'm not ready to react to that.
findings.context: Prospect is not ready to react to the quoted Growth/Enterprise pricing; OrbitFlow indicated Enterprise, not Growth, is the fit. — Pricing discussion; Growth starts at 1800/month for up to 30 users; Enterprise custom-priced.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Given your list, you're an Enterprise conversation, not a Growth one.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff stated Enterprise is the required tier given the prospect's list, and declined to quote a per-user figure until the user model is defined. — Vendor pricing position; prospect asked for itemised, user-based proposal to avoid surprises.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect wants licensing modelled on actual user population and asks for explicit seat treatment for occasional approvers, to avoid surprise costs. — Pricing/seat concern; a cost-related requirement for any proposal.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Concrete next steps then. We send the security pack
findings.context: Agreed next steps: OrbitFlow sends security pack and a written BAA position within a week; prospect sends representative workflow and sample data; joint pilot success criteria; permission-model session for Elliot. — Concrete next steps and pilot request.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm. But we could run a non-sensitive proof of concept in August
findings.context: Prospect sets timing: no production launch before Q4, but a non-sensitive proof of concept in August is possible. — Timeline and pilot request with explicit production constraint.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: One representative workflow working with real enough data. The security gates understood, and by understood I mean answered. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
findings.context: Decision requirements: one representative workflow working with real enough data, security gates answered, a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises, and operators believing they can own it. — Explicit decision criteria for moving to purchase.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I'm the sponsor — business systems. Security can veto, as you've seen. Privacy counsel reviews the DPA and the BAA. Procurement handles final terms.
findings.context: Decision-making process: Priya is sponsor; security can veto; privacy counsel reviews DPA and BAA; procurement handles final terms (four gates). — Named decision makers and approval process.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have. Those are the real competitors, not another workflow vendor.
findings.context: Competitive alternatives named by prospect: Power Automate (already covered by Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement) or improving existing process; OrbitFlow acknowledged a valid outcome is not buying. — Objection/competition; procurement sensitivity to existing licensing.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I'd say eleven weeks for anything non-trivial. It was six in January.
findings.context: Prospect's expressed value: the backlog (eleven weeks) and systems-group coordination cost; interest in a pilot baselined on systems-group hours. — Stated pain that drives purchase intent.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A demo with clean data proves nothing.
findings.context: Prospect's current interest in a pilot is conditional on the BAA position and on messy-data testing; prospect says a demo with clean data proves nothing. — Conditional interest and evaluation requirement.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to give you a yes on this call.
findings.context: Inferred: purchase likelihood is conditional and early-stage; the BAA blocker must be resolved before commercial progress, with OrbitFlow not giving a yes on the call. — Vendor declined to commit on BAA during call.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Customer states budget expectation well below the vendor's Growth price; sees the price gap as a blocker. — Prospect's own budget expectation versus Growth tier list price; objection to price.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: That's a real gap. I'm not going to pretend it isn't.
findings.context: Vendor acknowledges the price gap and says annual prepay gives only a meaningful discount, not a halving of cost. — Vendor response to budget objection; limits on discount.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
findings.context: Customer asks whether annual prepay would materially change the number, showing willingness to explore a lower-cost structure. — Potential negotiation lever raised by prospect.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
findings.context: Decision authority: prospect can approve tools under £15k/year alone; the Growth price (about £21.6k/year) goes to the COO and finance director, a slower process. — Approval process and named decision makers; price places deal above her authority.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Ideally something in place by early October, because after that nobody's changing anything until January.
findings.context: Prospect's target timeline: clean up automations and have something in place by early October, with a decision around August. — Timeline driven by holiday peak and company change freeze in November.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership. That's a real outcome and it might be the right one.
findings.context: Prospect names budget as the biggest risk and states a no-purchase outcome (keep Zapier and improve documentation) is a real possibility. — Objection / blocker; competitive alternative is the status quo tools.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I like the monitoring. I like the reusable templates. That's the bit that speaks to our actual problem. I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Prospect expresses interest in the product's monitoring and reusable templates, but is not yet convinced value closes the gap versus existing tools; says she is not saying no. — Mixed interest; positive on core features, undecided on value.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Then yes. Send me that.
findings.context: Prospect agreed to next steps: Marcus logs time on broken automations for four weeks; vendor sends written answers on Shopify trigger coverage and EU processing region and a rebuild of three worst automations. — Agreed next steps with no purchase commitment; decision still pending.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
findings.context: Prospect states the Shopify native trigger is a must-have; vendor could not confirm coverage and deferred it to a written answer. — Technical blocker unresolved; could stop purchase if polling-based.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Enterprise. That's the expensive one.
findings.context: Prospect says EU data residency on Enterprise is the expensive tier, a cost concern; vendor says residency is only on Enterprise. — Pricing tier implication for UK/EU compliance requirement.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: I genuinely don't know. Nobody's ever asked me to count it.
findings.context: Prospect's cost-of-status-quo case is not yet quantified; Marcus does not know the cost of the current setup and the team will count it for four weeks. — Business case gap; supports a slower decision.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Okay. That is the most compelling thing you've said.
findings.context: Prospect's sense of value: the template/subflow approach is the most compelling thing the vendor has said. — Positive buying signal on product value.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
findings.context: Vendor says usage pricing depends on workflow runs and premium connectors and will be modelled for the prospect's volumes; prospect is wary of hidden costs. — Pricing structure concern raised by prospect.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'd rather have a considered maybe than an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement.
findings.context: Vendor's own view: the deal may not close, and the vendor prefers an honest maybe to an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement. — Vendor framing of purchase likelihood; tone suggests cautious outlook.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Formal architecture review in September. Procurement in Q4. Realistic production use early next year.
findings.context: Customer states a timeline for formal architecture review, procurement, and production use, with production possibly early next year. — Timing signal from DeltaWorks; customer frames it as realistic and slow, not a committed date.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Architecture board first, and that is the one that matters. If architecture says no, nothing else happens.
findings.context: Customer names the decision process and sequence: architecture board first (can say no), information security in parallel, works council only if needed, procurement last. — Named decision makers and approval process; six stakeholders involved.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: If the answer is "possible but requires nine months of integration work", then the first use case is too heavy and we should choose a different first use case or not proceed.
findings.context: Customer identifies architecture viability for SAP and on-premise systems as the crux of whether to proceed; if too heavy, they would pick another first use case or not proceed. — Key blocker/condition on purchase; customer also notes MuleSoft-based alternative as a possible competing path.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I see strategic potential here. But I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
findings.context: Customer sees strategic potential but does not think a sandbox is the next step; wants architecture material first, then sandbox and pilot only if deployment is viable. — Next-step agreement; pilot is conditional, not requested yet.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: You will have all three by the end of next week.
findings.context: Agreed next steps: customer sends SAP operations list, promotion process doc, and arranges SAP interface owner hour; OrbitFlow sends security pack and architecture note, and returns within two weeks. — Concrete mutual action items with dates.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software.
findings.context: Customer says the headline licence price is not a surprise and cares most about transparency on services, premium connectors, and post-architecture costs; OrbitFlow commits to itemised pricing. — Pricing discussion; enterprise budget posture implied but no budget figure given.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Not headcount. I want to be very clear about that
findings.context: Customer says the business case is cycle time and error reduction, not headcount, and that a mismatch-catching use case has meaningful value though no number is yet available. — Value case for buying; savings figure not confirmed.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Six is realistic if the use case is contested.
findings.context: Customer lists blockers: SAP and on-premise connectivity, works council timing (up to six months if contested), regional IT, and procurement; a second use case (31+ Python scripts) is deferred to phase two. — Objections that could stall purchase; procurement described as slow and standard.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
findings.context: OrbitFlow positions itself as an Enterprise-tier opportunity, custom priced, and does not quote a number before user model is defined. — Vendor pricing position; no budget or price accepted by customer.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
findings.context: Customer requests explicit licensing treatment of occasional approvers so they do not require full seats, a condition on cost acceptability. — Pricing concern raised by governance lead; commitment from vendor to be explicit.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Because a sandbox would show me the product works, and I already believe the product works.
findings.context: Customer says the sandbox would not answer the key question and they are not yet ready for it; a sandbox request is deferred behind architecture. — Pilot/trial request explicitly declined for now.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Ours will not turn into the following June. It may turn into March.
findings.context: Customer says the timeline may land around March and will not slip to the following June, signalling urgency but also contingency. — Inferred from exchange; customer ties timing to architecture outcome.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: we're running this as a bake-off. You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks. This isn't a discovery call for us, we know what we want.
findings.context: Customer states the evaluation is a formal bake-off against Tray.io and that they already know what they want; they are testing whether OrbitFlow can do it. — Strong evaluation-stage intent; competitive pilot already running with Tray.io

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: I'm the executive sponsor and I'm broadly positive. Hannah and platform engineering score technical fit. Then security, legal, procurement, and the COO approve. So there are a lot of ways for this to die and only one way for it to happen.
findings.context: Customer sponsor says he is broadly positive, but multiple approval gates (technical fit, security, legal, procurement, COO) could stop the deal. — Named decision makers and approval process; objection/blocker risk

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Hannah Cole identifies herself as the most likely deal-killer, with model-risk and auditability as gating objections. — Blocker; conditional on satisfying model-risk and audit requirements

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It has a remediation programme, which has a budget, which is a number. Yes.
findings.context: Customer says the current manual/script process is a compliance problem driving the project, with a remediation programme that has a budget. — Budget and urgency signal: audit finding with a funded remediation programme

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Technical bake-off in July. Vendor decision in August. First controlled production workflows in October.
findings.context: Customer sets a decision timeline: technical bake-off in July, vendor decision in August, first controlled production workflows in October, driven by a remediation deadline. — Explicit timeline and deadline for purchase decision

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Assuming the security material lines up, I want to move. Send sandbox access and a written proposal for a six-week pilot so we can compare it against Tray properly rather than impressionistically.
findings.context: Customer says they want to move forward and requests sandbox access and a written six-week pilot proposal, conditional on security material. — Pilot request and agreed next step

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
findings.context: Customer is concerned about unpredictable usage overage costs in year two, and asks whether usage can be capped; OrbitFlow declines to promise a cap before modelling. — Pricing objection/concern; contract discussion

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — you're Enterprise, which is custom priced
findings.context: OrbitFlow quotes Growth at $1,800/month up to 30 users on annual agreement, but says the customer is an Enterprise shape with custom pricing; per-seat split for builders vs approvers to be itemised. — Pricing discussion; per-seat licensing concern

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
findings.context: Customer says the commercial range is roughly where expected for an enterprise workflow product and is not their concern. — Price acceptance signal

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Nothing binding. But I'd like the overage modelling done in parallel rather than after
findings.context: Customer wants a 'no-cost' or minimal commitment step: nothing binding yet, and asks for overage modelling in parallel with the pilot. — Next step; no binding commitment before pilot

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
findings.context: Customer identifies a no-purchase alternative (keep scripts and document them better) that would be proposed internally; Hannah says it would not satisfy the auditor but could cause a two-month detour. — Objection/blocker: status-quo or cheaper internal alternative

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Customer says the deal depends on OrbitFlow winning on debugging experience and programmatic audit export; connector breadth is a tie with Tray. — Competitive buying criteria

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It's not a two-horse bake-off, it's a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start.
findings.context: Customer's qualification of the deal: 'a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start' (Tray leads on time in the PoC). — Competitive position; Tray has head start

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Let me list what we owe you. Security pack
findings.context: OrbitFlow agrees to produce a joint six-week pilot with written success criteria, a security pack, and an audit payload schema; customer will provide volume estimates by Friday. — Agreed next steps and pilot deliverables

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So — I'm interested. I'm not dismissing it. But I'm not ready to run a sandbox myself
findings.context: Prospect Imogen Price expressed interest in OrbitFlow while stating price and complexity are risks and that Zapier plus process discipline may be good enough. — Mixed signal: interest with a real chance of not buying; she frames it as a possibility, not a decision.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Prospect states a budget constraint: she can sign software contracts up to £20,000 a year, above which the founder must approve; OrbitFlow's Growth package is £1,800/month (about £21,500/year). — Pricing exceeds her signing authority, creating a required approval step with the founder.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
findings.context: Prospect called the price above what she had in mind and said pricing will decide the deal. — Price objection raised directly after the OrbitFlow price was stated.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Prospect asked for a smaller start (10 users) or monthly billing to prove the process before an annual commitment; OrbitFlow said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval and did not confirm. — Pilot-style request and pricing negotiation; the vendor's confirmation is still pending.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
findings.context: Prospect objects to paying for 20 unneeded seats on the 30-user package. — Per-seat objection; vendor deflected to 'paying for the platform'.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
findings.context: Prospect says the founder will ask what the extra value is versus Zapier, and she needs a better answer than 'more robust'; the vendor's governance/audit pitch was rejected as irrelevant to an agency. — Value justification blocker for the decision maker.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We've got a new client-services process launching in September.
findings.context: Prospect is moving toward a decision with a timeline: she wants OrbitFlow running before a September client-services process launch, and plans to share a recorded demo with the founder and ops manager. — Concrete deadline and decision-maker process; OrbitFlow said September was no problem.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yep, all of it. I'll get it over.
findings.context: OrbitFlow agreed to a tailored recorded demo (Loom) by end of week, and to send a reference and a written DPA on model training; these are agreed next steps. — Next steps promised by vendor; the demo use case is the prospect's own workflow.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all.
findings.context: Prospect's ops team has no dedicated IT and will administer the tool; she raised this as a fit concern. — Blocker on complexity; vendor said it is no-code.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: So if the pitch is "we'll standardise your onboarding", that's going to meet resistance from me.
findings.context: Prospect's second contact (Ben Foster) raised resistance to standardised onboarding and asked for written data-training assurances and SSO confirmation; these are open conditions for a purchase. — Stakeholder conditions; SSO-on-all-plans claim is unconfirmed by vendor.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I'd have to check.
findings.context: Vendor's reference story implied a buying precedent; prospect questioned whether the customer's onboarding problem was actually solved, and vendor could not confirm renewal. — Vendor claim about a similar deal; not verified and weakens the case for the prospect.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: I want to be honest that it's exploration, not a procurement process.
findings.context: Customer states the decision is exploration, not a procurement process, and no decision is realistic this year. — Stated timing and intent; undercuts near-term purchase likelihood.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
findings.context: Customer says a decision would fall in the next budget cycle, with budgeting for next fiscal year starting in October. — Stated timeline for a possible decision; conditional on roadmap and architecture conversation.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: I'd rather have a roadmap and architecture conversation than a commercial proposal at this point.
findings.context: Customer asks for a roadmap and architecture session rather than a commercial proposal, and says that if two items look right they would have something to take into budgeting. — Agreed next step; explicitly not a proposal request yet.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it.
findings.context: Customer says the first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue and OrbitFlow must be materially better to displace the embedded, approved Power Automate. — Objection/blocker to purchase; the incumbent is licensed, approved and liked by the platform team.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
findings.context: Customer says the Microsoft platform team will not want this and has killed things before; influence is formal but practical impact depends on objection strength. — Named blocker/influencer in decision process.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: Licensing model is a major concern: customer has hundreds of supervisors who should not need full seats, and says a seat model requiring them would end the evaluation. — Per-seat pricing objection; OrbitFlow declined to give a number.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
findings.context: Customer says the price might be defensible for central operations, but the licensing model is the key question. — Pricing discussion; conditional interest.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Six builders, several hundred approvers.
findings.context: Builder population is about six (four in Lucy's team plus two regional specialists) against several hundred approvers; OrbitFlow says this shape must be explicit in any proposal. — Seat-shape information for pricing; OrbitFlow quoted Growth at 1800 a month up to 30 users and Enterprise custom priced.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states it cannot beat bundled Power Automate licensing on price; the case must rest on operational cost. — Vendor concession; cost objection to purchase.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's the argument I'd have to make internally, yes.
findings.context: Customer's buying case depends on an internal argument that operational cost of debugging flows exceeds the licence delta; they plan to measure it. — Business case condition; the day-a-week figure was an estimate.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's a very good test, actually.
findings.context: Customer is open to a benchmark pilot: build remediation flow for one region, have another region adapt it, and compare against Power Automate. — Possible pilot/trial path; proposed by OrbitFlow, customer responded positively.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's a better thought than I'd had, honestly.

draft.answer: Ember Financial and Inkwell Learning show the strongest buying signals: both have dated timelines and defined pilots, though each remains conditional [C1][C2]. Juniper Cloud Tools and Acme Logistics are also moving toward evaluations or pilots, with real blockers [C3][C4]. Harbor Legal and BrightPath Health are conditional on gating items [C5][C6]. DeltaWorks, Cedar & Finch and Fable Media are mixed or slower [C7][C8][C9]. Greenline Energy Services looks least likely near term [C10].

claims.text: Ember Financial: Noah Williams runs a formal bake-off against Tray.io (which has a six-week head start), has a funded remediation programme, accepts the enterprise price range, and wants to move: he asked for sandbox access and a written six-week pilot proposal, conditional on security material. Timeline is July bake-off, August decision, October production. Risks include Hannah Cole's model-risk and audit gate, a cheaper keep-the-scripts alternative, and overage-cost worries.

Inkwell Learning: Olivia Grant wants a pilot before November renewal planning with a decision by late September, and defined a test on twenty historical escalations. She calls the price reasonable if it consolidates manual programmes, and Jon Bell called it the best-specified pilot he has seen this year. Darren Wu's backward data analysis is due end of next week and he says he would say no if the data does not support it. The analyst-style reading suggests moderate-to-strong intent (inferred).

Juniper Cloud Tools: Marcus Chen owns the budget and wants to proceed with a four-week evaluation and a September go/no-go, and the business problem is urgent. Ava Sinclair effectively holds a veto, says most of it could be built internally, and named blockers (unreadable exports, individually billed subflows, Postgres connector). Marcus said that if engineering questions cannot be answered they should not buy.

Acme Logistics: Rachel Morgan is interested enough to test and would supply three real workflows if given a sandbox, aiming to choose a vendor by end of July. Blockers are price needing a clearer ROI story, the question of expanding the existing Workato contract instead, and per-seat clarity. Next steps are a security pack and jointly written pilot criteria. Security is not seen as the gating issue.

Harbor Legal: Eleanor Brooks is interested in the governance capabilities and comfortable with the enterprise price range, and scope is two practice groups with a possible Q4 proof of concept. Samir Khan holds a veto, is sceptical about integration effort versus value, and if every partner needs a seat it would be a very short conversation. Sentiment appears cautiously positive but conditional (inferred).

BrightPath Health: Priya Shah would still consider a limited pilot and a non-sensitive August proof of concept, but the BAA is a hard gate, procurement will not discuss price until it is answered, and there is no production before Q4. OrbitFlow did not give a yes on the BAA. Likelihood appears conditional and early-stage (inferred).

DeltaWorks Manufacturing: Martin Vogel sees strategic potential and is not surprised by licence price, but the architecture board can say no, SAP/on-premise viability is the crux, and he declined a sandbox for now. Timeline: architecture review in September, procurement in Q4, production early next year.

Cedar & Finch: Sophie Reed likes monitoring and templates, but Growth pricing is far above her expected budget of about eight hundred to a thousand a month and above her approval limit. She names budget as the biggest risk, with keeping Zapier a real outcome; the Shopify trigger is a must-have. The vendor, Leo Grant, preferred a considered maybe (inferred caution).

Fable Media: Imogen Price is interested and wants OrbitFlow running before a September launch, but says price is above what she had in mind and exceeds her signing authority, so the founder must approve. Zapier is a possible alternative, and she objects to paying for seats she does not need.

Greenline Energy Services: Carlos Mendes says it is exploration, not procurement, and a decision would fall in the budget cycle starting in October. The Microsoft platform team will resist, there is a first-class Dynamics gap, and a seat model requiring supervisors would end the evaluation. Near-term likelihood appears low (inferred).

conflicts.description: Carlos is open to a benchmark pilot and the price may be defensible, yet says it is exploration and realistically no near-term decision.
The sponsor is broadly positive and wants to move, but Hannah Cole describes Tray as having a six-week head start and a cheaper alternative could be proposed.

evidence.context: Ava names concrete blockers that would stop a purchase: unreadable exported definitions, subflows billed individually, and a Postgres connector that misbehaves. — Conditions that would block purchase, stated by the technical evaluator.

claims.text: Acme Logistics: Rachel Morgan is interested enough to test and would supply three real workflows if given a sandbox, aiming to choose a vendor by end of July. Blockers are price needing a clearer ROI story, the question of expanding the existing Workato contract instead, and per-seat clarity. Next steps are a security pack and jointly written pilot criteria. Security is not seen as the gating issue.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows
evidence.context: Customer expressed interest in testing the product: will supply three real workflows if given a sandbox. — Pilot request and buying signal from the prospect after the call; conditional on exception handling holding up.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: That's the intent. It'll slip. It always slips. But that's the plan.
evidence.context: Customer stated a timeline: choose a vendor before end of July and first workflows live in September, but acknowledged it will slip. — Timeline and decision deadline; Maya's question framed the date, Rachel confirmed it as the intent.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story
evidence.context: Customer said the price could still be justified only with a clearer ROI story, so cost is a blocker unless ROI is made concrete. — Objection tied to cost; customer also named potential offset from Gainsight spend.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
evidence.context: Main commercial blocker: customer must win internally on expanding its existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Competing alternative and internal approval risk, raised as the real commercial question.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer asked that per-seat licensing be explicit, worried that occasional approvers would need full seats. — Licence and per-seat pricing concern; OrbitFlow agreed to itemise builders and viewer/approver populations.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
evidence.context: Next steps agreed: vendor sends security pack and architecture summary; customer sends representative workflow and sample data; jointly write three to five pilot success criteria before deciding on sandbox. — Agreed next steps toward a pilot.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
evidence.context: Security review is not a blocker; the customer said the gating issue is not security, and Tom said AI concerns should not block the automation case. — Objection assessment; AI security review could be separated.

claims.text: Harbor Legal: Eleanor Brooks is interested in the governance capabilities and comfortable with the enterprise price range, and scope is two practice groups with a possible Q4 proof of concept. Samir Khan holds a veto, is sceptical about integration effort versus value, and if every partner needs a seat it would be a very short conversation. Sentiment appears cautiously positive but conditional (inferred).

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: The governance side interests me. Genuinely. The run history, the approval logging, the connection scoping Samir liked — that's better than what we have
evidence.context: Customer expressed enthusiasm for the phase-one governance capabilities (run history, approval logging, connection scoping) as better than current state. — Positive buying signal from Eleanor Brooks, but framed as interest in governance rather than a purchase commitment.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: The enterprise range itself doesn't worry me. We buy expensive software.
evidence.context: Pricing: OrbitFlow staff stated Growth tier is 1800 per month up to thirty users annually, but the customer's needs fall under Enterprise, which is custom priced. Customer says the enterprise range does not worry them. — Pricing discussion; Eleanor is comfortable with enterprise price range, but licensing split for partner seats is unresolved and could make it a very short conversation.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: A firm-wide process change on top of a new platform is two changes and we'd fail at both.
evidence.context: Scope agreed to be two practice groups rather than the whole firm, which customer says is needed to make it an easier conversation; a firm-wide change would fail. — Customer-driven scoping that reduces blast radius and makes approval easier.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Possible proof of concept in Q4. Broader rollout would be next year.
evidence.context: Timeline: a possible proof of concept in Q4 with broader rollout next year; decision in Q1 agreed as the honest shape. December and January are constrained. — Timing signal; Eleanor cautions nothing significant happens in December and January is taken by annual planning.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Customer's stated reservation is integration effort versus value; this is the main objection that could stop a purchase. — Samir Khan flagged this as the biggest risk; the concern is that security constraints plus lack of native legal connectors make integration disproportionate.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: And I'm much more sceptical about generative AI than Eleanor is.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks described the reservation as Samir's, and Samir confirmed he is more sceptical about generative AI than she is. — Shows internal disagreement between decision-makers; Samir has veto power as security and risk.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
evidence.context: Blocker: if partners each need a seat, the deal could be very short; the licensing split is needed in writing before any internal commitment. — Per-seat licensing objection risk, raised by customer.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: That was more useful than I expected, and I say that having been quite sceptical about this meeting.
evidence.context: Inferred: customer's sentiment is cautiously positive but conditional, with multiple written gating items outstanding before a purchase decision. — Overall tone; Eleanor says meeting was more useful than expected, but the reservation and gates remain.

claims.text: BrightPath Health: Priya Shah would still consider a limited pilot and a non-sensitive August proof of concept, but the BAA is a hard gate, procurement will not discuss price until it is answered, and there is no production before Q4. OrbitFlow did not give a yes on the BAA. Likelihood appears conditional and early-stage (inferred).

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data. But I want to be explicit about something: a successful pilot would not automatically mean we can deploy broadly.
evidence.context: BrightPath's sponsor would still consider a limited pilot, but a successful pilot does not automatically mean broad deployment; these are two decisions with different approvers. — Buying signal tempered by explicit separation of pilot vs. broad deployment decisions.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm. But we could run a non-sensitive proof of concept in August
evidence.context: Prospect sets timing: no production launch before Q4, but a non-sensitive proof of concept in August is possible. — Timeline and pilot request with explicit production constraint.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
evidence.context: Prospect's stated decision gate: the BAA is a hard gate; without one, OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow that may involve PHI. — Primary blocker to any purchase; security/BAA must be answered before pricing matters.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
evidence.context: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security confirms whether the BAA requirement can be met; price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Pricing/contract discussion deferred; objection to commercial discussion now.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'm not going to give you a yes on this call.
evidence.context: Inferred: purchase likelihood is conditional and early-stage; the BAA blocker must be resolved before commercial progress, with OrbitFlow not giving a yes on the call. — Vendor declined to commit on BAA during call.

claims.text: DeltaWorks Manufacturing: Martin Vogel sees strategic potential and is not surprised by licence price, but the architecture board can say no, SAP/on-premise viability is the crux, and he declined a sandbox for now. Timeline: architecture review in September, procurement in Q4, production early next year.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: I see strategic potential here. But I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
evidence.context: Customer sees strategic potential but does not think a sandbox is the next step; wants architecture material first, then sandbox and pilot only if deployment is viable. — Next-step agreement; pilot is conditional, not requested yet.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software.
evidence.context: Customer says the headline licence price is not a surprise and cares most about transparency on services, premium connectors, and post-architecture costs; OrbitFlow commits to itemised pricing. — Pricing discussion; enterprise budget posture implied but no budget figure given.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Architecture board first, and that is the one that matters. If architecture says no, nothing else happens.
evidence.context: Customer names the decision process and sequence: architecture board first (can say no), information security in parallel, works council only if needed, procurement last. — Named decision makers and approval process; six stakeholders involved.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: If the answer is "possible but requires nine months of integration work", then the first use case is too heavy and we should choose a different first use case or not proceed.
evidence.context: Customer identifies architecture viability for SAP and on-premise systems as the crux of whether to proceed; if too heavy, they would pick another first use case or not proceed. — Key blocker/condition on purchase; customer also notes MuleSoft-based alternative as a possible competing path.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Because a sandbox would show me the product works, and I already believe the product works.
evidence.context: Customer says the sandbox would not answer the key question and they are not yet ready for it; a sandbox request is deferred behind architecture. — Pilot/trial request explicitly declined for now.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Formal architecture review in September. Procurement in Q4. Realistic production use early next year.
evidence.context: Customer states a timeline for formal architecture review, procurement, and production use, with production possibly early next year. — Timing signal from DeltaWorks; customer frames it as realistic and slow, not a committed date.

claims.text: Cedar & Finch: Sophie Reed likes monitoring and templates, but Growth pricing is far above her expected budget of about eight hundred to a thousand a month and above her approval limit. She names budget as the biggest risk, with keeping Zapier a real outcome; the Shopify trigger is a must-have. The vendor, Leo Grant, preferred a considered maybe (inferred caution).

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I like the monitoring. I like the reusable templates. That's the bit that speaks to our actual problem. I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
evidence.context: Prospect expresses interest in the product's monitoring and reusable templates, but is not yet convinced value closes the gap versus existing tools; says she is not saying no. — Mixed interest; positive on core features, undecided on value.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
evidence.context: Customer states budget expectation well below the vendor's Growth price; sees the price gap as a blocker. — Prospect's own budget expectation versus Growth tier list price; objection to price.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
evidence.context: Decision authority: prospect can approve tools under £15k/year alone; the Growth price (about £21.6k/year) goes to the COO and finance director, a slower process. — Approval process and named decision makers; price places deal above her authority.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership. That's a real outcome and it might be the right one.
evidence.context: Prospect names budget as the biggest risk and states a no-purchase outcome (keep Zapier and improve documentation) is a real possibility. — Objection / blocker; competitive alternative is the status quo tools.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Prospect states the Shopify native trigger is a must-have; vendor could not confirm coverage and deferred it to a written answer. — Technical blocker unresolved; could stop purchase if polling-based.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: I'd rather have a considered maybe than an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement.
evidence.context: Vendor's own view: the deal may not close, and the vendor prefers an honest maybe to an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement. — Vendor framing of purchase likelihood; tone suggests cautious outlook.

claims.text: Fable Media: Imogen Price is interested and wants OrbitFlow running before a September launch, but says price is above what she had in mind and exceeds her signing authority, so the founder must approve. Zapier is a possible alternative, and she objects to paying for seats she does not need.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So — I'm interested. I'm not dismissing it. But I'm not ready to run a sandbox myself
evidence.context: Prospect Imogen Price expressed interest in OrbitFlow while stating price and complexity are risks and that Zapier plus process discipline may be good enough. — Mixed signal: interest with a real chance of not buying; she frames it as a possibility, not a decision.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We've got a new client-services process launching in September.
evidence.context: Prospect is moving toward a decision with a timeline: she wants OrbitFlow running before a September client-services process launch, and plans to share a recorded demo with the founder and ops manager. — Concrete deadline and decision-maker process; OrbitFlow said September was no problem.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
evidence.context: Prospect called the price above what she had in mind and said pricing will decide the deal. — Price objection raised directly after the OrbitFlow price was stated.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Prospect states a budget constraint: she can sign software contracts up to £20,000 a year, above which the founder must approve; OrbitFlow's Growth package is £1,800/month (about £21,500/year). — Pricing exceeds her signing authority, creating a required approval step with the founder.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
evidence.context: Prospect objects to paying for 20 unneeded seats on the 30-user package. — Per-seat objection; vendor deflected to 'paying for the platform'.

claims.text: Greenline Energy Services: Carlos Mendes says it is exploration, not procurement, and a decision would fall in the budget cycle starting in October. The Microsoft platform team will resist, there is a first-class Dynamics gap, and a seat model requiring supervisors would end the evaluation. Near-term likelihood appears low (inferred).

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: I want to be honest that it's exploration, not a procurement process.
evidence.context: Customer states the decision is exploration, not a procurement process, and no decision is realistic this year. — Stated timing and intent; undercuts near-term purchase likelihood.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
evidence.context: Customer says a decision would fall in the next budget cycle, with budgeting for next fiscal year starting in October. — Stated timeline for a possible decision; conditional on roadmap and architecture conversation.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
evidence.context: Customer says the Microsoft platform team will not want this and has killed things before; influence is formal but practical impact depends on objection strength. — Named blocker/influencer in decision process.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it.
evidence.context: Customer says the first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue and OrbitFlow must be materially better to displace the embedded, approved Power Automate. — Objection/blocker to purchase; the incumbent is licensed, approved and liked by the platform team.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
evidence.context: Licensing model is a major concern: customer has hundreds of supervisors who should not need full seats, and says a seat model requiring them would end the evaluation. — Per-seat pricing objection; OrbitFlow declined to give a number.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Realistically, no.
evidence.context: Inferred: overall purchase likelihood in the near term is low; the customer is interested but early, with the main blockers being the Microsoft platform team, incumbent licensing, and the lack of a first-class Dynamics connector. — Synthesis of stated objections and timing; not a customer statement.

conflicts.description: Carlos is open to a benchmark pilot and the price may be defensible, yet says it is exploration and realistically no near-term decision.
The sponsor is broadly positive and wants to move, but Hannah Cole describes Tray as having a six-week head start and a cheaper alternative could be proposed.

not_covered: No actual purchase outcomes or probabilities are in the findings; this is a judgement from signals only.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as calls of type Prospect (new business), excluding renewals, churned customers and cold calls.
Likelihood to purchase is a judgement across calls, so each call is read for underlying buying signals rather than a ranking.
Prospects means calls of type Prospect only, excluding renewals, churned customers and cold calls.
Likelihood is a judgement from buying signals, not a ranking from the data.
